provenance.note: SLOT 20 IS THE BINARY'S OWN WORD. Routine 0 is six instructions: `move.l a3,$228(a5)` for the data block, `move.l a0,$230(a5)` for a REMOVE routine that is a bare `rts`, and `moveq #$13,d0`. `ExtAdr` is $f8 with sixteen bytes a slot (+Equ.s:1185), so ($228-$f8)/16+1 = 20 and $13 is 19, the slot zero-based. The readme says the same from the outside -- "It should be added as extension number 20" -- and so does ExoticA's AMOS extensions wiki.

findings: REPLACES AN AMOSTOOLS STUB. Until 2026-08-12 this row held only the token table with the library stripped out from under it -- both length fields zero, no code, every routine word overwritten with `====` -- so the tier could not rise above `manual`. The real library's table is IDENTICAL to the stub's, entry for entry, id for id and spec for spec, which is a check on the AMOSTools reader as much as on this registration. THE LIBRARY IS CALLED `Tiny.lib` and nothing about that filename says which extension it is -- it was identified from its token table, which carries `opengui`, `closegui`, `wait`, `waitport`, `getimsg`, `replyimsg`, `gotoamos`, `gotowb`, this row's names exactly. 1,208 bytes, the smallest library registered. WHAT IT IS FOR, and it explains the odd keyword names: OrgAsm is a TRANSLATOR, not a GUI library. In the author's words it "'sits' between two other programs, namely GadToolsBox and A68k" -- you paint an interface in GadToolsBox, save it as assembler, and OrgAsm rewrites that source into something AMOS can use and assembles it into Ram:GUI.BIN and Ram:GUI.ASC. The extension is only the runtime that loads the resulting blob and pumps its message port, which is why fourteen keywords is enough and why they are spelled `f<opengui>` rather than `Open Gui`. THE SHIPPED BUILD IS THE DEMO, and it says so twice: the title string at $46b reads `T-SOFT Demo extension V 1.0`, and both `f<opengui>` ($2ae) and `f<closegui>` ($30c) call intuition's `DisplayAlert` (-$5a, intuition_lib.fd) with `d0 = 0`, the height `$3e` and a four-line message at block+$c: "Recoverable Alert: Press any mouse button", "Do yourself a favour, buy a copy of Liberator,", "a great new extension for Amos. Please contact", "T-SOFT, PO Box 598, Ayr KA6 6PJ United Kingdom". A red Intuition alert over the whole display, on every open and every close. EVERY KEYWORD IS A DIRECT AMIGAOS CALL, and the LVOs are read out of the corpus `.fd` files rather than recalled: exec `Wait` (-$13e, routine 3), `WaitPort` (-$180), `OpenLibrary` (-$228) and `CloseLibrary` (-$19e); gadtools `GT_GetIMsg` (-$48) and `GT_ReplyIMsg` (-$4e); intuition `ItemAddress` (-$90) and the alert above. `f<gotoamos>` and `f<gotowb>` are one AMOS call each, `AMOS_WB` at $120(a0) with d1 = 1 and 0. And `f<opengui>` and `f<closegui>` END IN `jsr (a0)`, into the GadToolsBox blob a program Bloaded into bank 8 -- 68k machine code out of an AMOS bank, which is the boundary `Call` sits on and which this port does not cross. That is what blocks the row: intuition.library, gadtools.library and 68k execution, three back-ends, and the two keywords that build the interface at all are the ones behind the third. A DEFECT IN THE SHIPPED TABLE: `f<wait>`'s entry names routine 953 in a fifteen-routine jump table, so the keyword jumps off the end of it. Routine 3 IS `Wait(signalSet)` and no token names it, which is where the entry was meant to point. The readme's worked example sends multi-window programs straight at it, telling a program watching more than one window to sleep on `F<wait>` where `F<waitport>` serves a single one -- not quoted, because that sentence lives inside the example as five `Rem` lines and exists nowhere as one string. The six example programs (1_Buttons through 6-TooMany, 6KB to 14KB) are the only demonstration of what the keywords do -- the readme documents the translator, not the runtime.
notes: Demo of a GUI toolkit built on intuition.library and gadtools.library.
